item.title: NSPP plasma-water graphene oxide
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported for the lab method (peer-reviewed). Cost, tonne-scale, and “replaces graphite” claims are Preliminary. The 1 Oct 2026 Chemical Engineering item is a recurrence of a paper accepted February 2026.

Related notes: [[guides/glossary|NSPP]] · [[topics/health/form-route|GO]] · [[reference/production]]

Five facts

  1. Banavath et al. grow graphene oxide at a methane–water interface with a non-thermal atmospheric nanosecond pulsed plasma (NSPP). No mined graphite, no Hummers acids.
  2. Journal: Nature Communications, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-69831-0. Received 9 Aug 2025, accepted 9 Feb 2026. Texas A&M plus LTEOIL (College Station).
  3. Reported lab rate: a four-gap reactor up to about 5 g GO per day. That is a bench scale-up, not a plant.
  4. Hydrogen is the co-product. The project started as a hydrogen effort; carbon sheets were the unexpected high-value solid.
  5. Trade coverage on 1 Oct 2026 (Chemical Engineering) restates the July 2026 university release. It is not a new experiment.

What the process is

Conventional GO starts with graphite, oxidizes it (Brodie, Staudenmaier, Hummers and variants), then exfoliates. That route needs concentrated acids and leaves a waste stream.

item.title: Holey graphene as a molecular stencil
item.description:
Evidence: Well-supported (peer-reviewed method paper). The mid-September 2026 news cycle is a recurrence, not a new isolation of graphene.

Related notes: [[topics/engineering/2026-09-15-ucla-graphene-stencil]] · [[weekly/2026-W38]] · [[recurrence/log]] · [[timeline/2004]]

If you only remember five facts

  1. The method is a mask: graphene covers gold except at engineered holes; thiol-bearing molecules bind gold in the holes and are blocked where intact graphene sits.
  2. The landmark paper is Thomas et al., ACS Nano 9, 10909 (2015), DOI 10.1021/acsnano.5b03936 — “Holey Graphene as a Weed Barrier for Molecules.”
  3. UCLA Health recirculated the same press framing on 14–15 September 2026. Authors named in that release match the 2015 paper (Paul Weiss, John Thomas, Shan Jiang, Nathan Weiss, Xiangfeng Duan, plus Caltech theory from Gethers and Goddard).
  4. Goal stated by the team: patterned nanoelectronic / biosensor surfaces, including devices small enough in principle to think about recording brain-relevant signals. That is a research aim, not a shipped implant.
  5. Graphene here is used for what it blocks (a chemically quiet lid) as much as for what it conducts.

What “stencil” means in this lab

Chemists have long known how to stick molecules to gold. A thiol (–SH) head group binds Au strongly and can form a self-assembled monolayer (SAM). That is a feature and a problem: gold will accept those molecules almost everywhere the surface is clean. If you want a pattern — molecules only in 20-nanometre-class patches, not a uniform film — you need a mask.

item.title: How publishing works
item.description:
Three places, one piece of writing.

1. Archive

The public file history lives in GrapheneFacts/graphene-archive. That repo is for storage, diffs, and source links — not for comfortable reading.

Private compile work stays in the private repo and does not go on this site.

2. This site

Readable pages are Markdown files under content/ in GrapheneFacts/quartz. A push to the v5 branch rebuilds graphenefacts.github.io/quartz.

Each essay can link back to the archive file it came from.

item.title: Welcome to the GrapheneFacts reading site
item.description:
GitHub is the archive. This page is what readers should open first.

Each write-up here is a Markdown file in content/. The same file history lives in Git. Longer source dumps and X-post copies can stay in the public archive.

See also [[topics/graphene]] and [[about]].
